Good-bye for the present; I won’t intrude upon friends in council.
What in the devil’s name do you want here?
I must speak to you. You promised me yesterday an account of the founding of the League, and——
I can’t give it you; it must wait till another time.
Impossible, Mr. Stensgård; the paper appears to-morrow morning.
Nonsense! It has all to be altered. The matter has entered on a new phase; new forces have come into play. What I said about Chamberlain Bratsberg must be entirely recast before it can appear.
Oh, that about the Chamberlain, that’s in type already.
Then it must come out of type again.
I won’t have it published in that form. Why do you stare at me? Do you think I don’t know how to manage the affairs of the League?
Oh, certainly; but you must let me tell you——
No arguing, Aslaksen; that I can’t and won’t stand!
Do you know, Mr. Stensgård, that you are doing your best to take the bread out of my mouth? Do you know that?
No; I know nothing of the sort.
But you are. Last winter, before you came here, my paper was looking up. I edited it myself, I must tell you, and I edited it on a principle.

Yes, I!—I said to myself: it’s the great public that supports a paper; now the great public is the bad public—that comes of the local situation; and the bad public will have a bad paper. So you see I edited it——

Well, and I prospered by it. But then you came and brought ideas into the district. The paper took on a colour, and then Lundestad’s supporters all fell away. The subscribers that are left won’t pay their subscriptions——
Ah, but the paper has become a good one.

I can’t live on a good paper. You were to make things lively; you were to grapple with abuses, as you promised yesterday. The bigwigs were to be pilloried; the paper was to be filled with things people were bound to read—and now, you leave me in the lurch——
Ho-ho! You think I am going to keep you supplied with libels! No, thank you, my good sir!
Mr. Stensgård, you musn’t drive me to desperation, or you’ll repent it.

I mean that I must make the paper pay in another way. Heaven knows I should be sorry to do it. Before you came I made an honest living out of accidents and suicides and other harmless things, that often hadn’t even happened. But now you have turned everything topsy-turvy; people now want very different fare——

Just let me tell you this: if you break loose in any way, if you go a single step beyond my orders, and try to exploit the movement in your own dirty interests, I’ll go to the opposition printer and start a new paper. We have money, you must know! We can bring your rag to ruin in a fortnight.
Yes, I would; and you’ll see I can edit a paper so as to appeal to the great public.
Then I’ll go this instant to Chamberlain Bratsberg——
You? What have you to do with him?

What have you to do with him? Do you think I don’t know why you are invited here? It’s because he is afraid of you, and of what you may do; and you are making capital of that. But if he’s afraid of what you may do, he’ll be no less afraid of what I may print; and I will make capital of that!
Would you dare to? A wretched creature like you——!
I’ll soon show you. If your speech is to be kept out of the paper, the Chamberlain shall pay me for keeping it out.
Try it; just try it! You’re drunk, fellow——!
Only in moderation. But I’ll fight like a lion if you try to take my poor crust out of my mouth. Little you know what sort of a home mine is: a bedridden wife, a crippled child——

Off with you! Do you think I want to be soiled with your squalor? What are your bedridden wives and deformed brats to me? If you stand in my way, if you dare so much as to obstruct a single one of my prospects, you shall be on the parish before the year’s out!
Ah, you’re coming to your senses.
I shall announce to the subscribers in a handbill that in consequence of an indisposition contracted at the fête, the editor——
Yes, do so; I daresay, later on, we shall come to an understanding.
I trust we may.—Remember this, Mr. Stensgård: that paper is my one ewe lamb.
[At the foremost garden door.] Ah, Mr. Stensgård!
You here alone? If you have no objection, I should like to have a little talk with you.
In the first place, let me say that if any one has told you that I have said anything to your disadvantage, you musn’t believe it.
To my disadvantage? What do you mean?
Oh, nothing; nothing, I assure you. You see, there are so many busybodies here, that go about doing nothing but setting people by the ears.
Well, on the whole—I’m afraid our relations are a little strained.
They are quite natural relations, Mr. Stensgård: the relation of the old to the new; it is always so.
Oh, come, Mr. Lundestad, you are not so old as all that.
Yes indeed, I’m getting old. I have held my seat ever since 1839. It’s time I should be relieved.
Times change, you see. New problems arise, and for their solution we want new forces.
Now, frankly, Mr. Lundestad—are you really going to give up your seat to Monsen?
To Monsen? No, certainly not to Monsen.
Suppose, now, I did retire in Monsen’s favour: do you think he would be elected?
It’s hard to say. As the preliminary election comes on the day after to-morrow, there may scarcely be time to prepare the public mind; but——

I don’t believe he would manage it. The Chamberlain’s party, my party, would not vote for him. Of course “my party” is a figure of speech; I mean the men of property, the old families, who are settled on their own land and belong to it. They won’t have anything to do with Monsen. Monsen is a newcomer; no one really knows anything about Monsen and his affairs. And then he has had to cut down so much to clear a place for himself—to fell both trees and men, you may say.
Well then, if you think he has no chance——
H’m! You are a man of rare gifts, Mr. Stensgård. Providence has dealt lavishly with you. But it has made one little oversight: it ought to have given you one thing more.
Tell me—why do you never think of yourself? Why have you no ambition?
Why do you waste all your strength on other people? In one word—why not go into Parliament yourself?
Why not? You have qualified, I hear. And if you don’t seize this opportunity, then some one else will come in; and when once he is firm in the saddle, it may not be so easy to unseat him.
Great heavens, Mr. Lundestad! do you really mean what you say?
Oh, I don’t want to commit you; if you don’t care about it——
Not care about it! Well, I must confess I’m not so utterly devoid of ambition as you suppose. But do you really think it possible?
Oh, there’s nothing impossible about it. I should do my best, and so, no doubt, would the Chamberlain; he knows your oratorical gifts. You have the young men on your side——
Mr. Lundestad, by heaven, you are my true friend!
Oh, you don’t mean much by that. If you really looked upon me as a friend, you would relieve me of this burden. You have young shoulders; you could bear it so easily.
I place myself entirely at your disposal; I will not fail you.
Then you are really not disinclined to——

Thanks! Believe me, Mr. Stensgård, you will not regret it. But now we must go warily to work. We must both of us take care to be on the electoral college—I to propose you as my successor, and put you through your facings before the rest; and you to give an account of your views——
If we once get so far, we are safe. In the electoral college you are omnipotent.
There is a limit to omnipotence. You must of course bring your oratory into play; you must take care to explain away anything that might seem really awkward or objectionable——
You don’t mean that I am to break with my party?

Now just look at the thing reasonably. What do we mean when we talk of two parties? We have, on the one hand, certain men or families who are in possession of the common civic advantages—I mean property, independence, and power. That is the party I belong to. On the other hand, we have the mass of our younger fellow citizens who want to share in these advantages. That is your party. But that party you will quite naturally and properly pass out of when you get into power—to say nothing of taking up a solid position as a man of property—for of course that is essential, Mr. Stensgård.
Yes, I believe it is. But the time is short; and such a position is not to be attained in a day.
That’s true; but perhaps the prospect of such a position would be enough——

Have you any rooted objection to a good marriage, Mr. Stensgård? There are heiresses in the country-side. A man like you, with a future before him—a man who can reckon on attaining the highest offices—believe me, you needn’t fear a repulse if you play your cards neatly.

Then, for heaven’s sake, help me in the game! You open wide vistas to me—great visions! All that I have hoped and longed for, and that seemed so dreamlike and far away, stands suddenly before me in living reality—to lead the people forward towards emancipation, to——

Yes, we must keep our eyes open, Mr. Stensgård. I see your ambition is already on the alert. That’s well. The rest will come of itself.—In the meantime, thanks! I shall never forget your readiness to take the burden of office from my old shoulders.
[The whole party gradually enters from the garden. Two maid-servants bring in candles and hand round refreshments during the following scene.
[Goes towards the piano at the back, left.] Mr. Stensgård, you must join us; we are going to have a game of forfeits.
With pleasure; I am just in the mood.
[Follows her towards the back, makes arrangements with her, places chairs, etc. etc.
[In an undertone.] What the deuce is this my father is saying, Mr. Heire? What speech has Mr. Stensgård been making yesterday?
Hee-hee! Don’t you know about it?
No; we townspeople had our dinner and ball at the Club. My father declares Mr. Stensgård has entirely broken with the Stonelee gang—that he was frightfully rude to Monsen——
To Monsen! No, you must have misunderstood him, my dear sir.
Well, there were a whole lot of people about, so that I couldn’t quite follow what he said; but I certainly heard——
Wait till to-morrow—— I say no more. You’ll have the whole story with your coffee, in Aslaksen’s paper.
Well, my dear Lundestad, are you sticking to those crotchets of yours?
They are no crotchets, Chamberlain; rather than be ousted, one should give way gracefully.
Nonsense; who is dreaming of ousting you?
H’m; I’m an old weather-prophet. There has been a change in the wind. Besides, I have my successor ready. Mr. Stensgård is willing——
Wasn’t that what you meant? I took it for a hint when you said he was a man we must make friends with and support.
I meant in his onslaught upon all the corruption and swindling that goes on at Stonelee.
But how could you count so confidently upon his breaking with that crew?
He did it openly enough last evening, my dear fellow.
Yes, when he spoke of Monsen’s deplorable influence in the district.
Of course; that time on the table——
He was frightfully rude; called him a money-bag, and a griffin or a basilisk, or something. Ha-ha!—it was great sport to hear him.
Yes, I own I’m not sorry to see these people a little roughly handled. But now we must back him up; for after such a savage attack——
As that of yesterday, you mean?
Yes, against Monsen and his set. Of course they’ll try to have their revenge; you can’t blame them——
[Decidedly.] Mr. Stensgård must be supported—that is clear!
Father dear, you must join in the game.
Yes, indeed you must; Selma insists upon it.

Very well, I suppose I must give in. [In an undertone as they go towards the back.] I’m quite distressed about Lundestad; he is really failing; fancy, he didn’t in the least understand what Stensgård——
Oh, come, come; they’ve begun the game.
[She drags him into the circle of young people where the game is in full swing.
[Calls from his place.] Mr. Heire, you are appointed forfeit-judge.
Hee-hee! It’s the first appointment I ever had.
[Also in the circle.] On account of your legal experience, Mr. Heire.
Oh, my amiable young friends, I should be delighted to sentence you all—— I say no more!
[Slips up to Lundestad, who stands in front on the left.] You were speaking to the Chamberlain. What about? Was it about me?
Unfortunately it was—about that affair of yesterday evening——
He said you had been frightfully rude.
Do you think it isn’t a torture to me?
Now is your chance to atone for it.
Coming! [Quickly to Lundestad.] What do you mean?
Find an opportunity and apologise to the Chamberlain.
[The game goes on with noise and laughter. Some elderly gentlemen play cards on the right. Lundestad takes a seat on the left; Daniel Heire near him.
That whelp twits me with my legal experience, does he?
He’s rather free with his tongue, that’s certain.
And so the whole family goes and fawns upon him. Hee-hee! They’re pitifully afraid of him.
No, there you are wrong, Mr. Heire; the Chamberlain is not afraid of him.
Not afraid? Do you think I’m blind, my good sir?
No, but—I can trust you to keep the secret? Well, I’ll tell you all about it. The Chamberlain thinks it was Monsen he was attacking.
Fact, Mr. Heire! Ringdal or Miss Thora must have got him persuaded that——
And so he goes and asks him to a state dinner-party! Deuce take me, if that isn’t the best thing I’ve heard for long! No, really now, I can’t keep that bottled up.
Sh, sh! Remember your promise. The Chamberlain’s your old school-fellow: and even if he has been a little hard upon you——
Hee-hee! I’ll pay him back with interest!
Take care! The Chamberlain is powerful. Don’t play tricks in the lion’s den!
Bratsberg a lion? Pooh, he’s a blockhead, sir, and I am not. Oh, won’t I get a rare crop of taunts, and jibes, and innuendoes out of this, when once our great suit comes on!
[Calls from the circle.] Learned judge, what shall the owner of this forfeit do?
[Unnoticed, to Heire.] It’s Stensgård’s! Think of something amusing.
That forfeit? Hee-hee, let me see; he might, for example—yes—he shall make a speech!
Mr. Stensgård is to make a speech.
Oh no, spare me that; I came off badly enough last night.
Excellently, Mr. Stensgård; I know something of public speaking.
[To Heire.] If only he doesn’t put his foot in it now.
Put his foot in it? Hee-hee! You’re a sharp one! That’s an inspiration! [In an undertone to Stensgård .] If you came off badly last night, why not put yourself right again to-night?
[Seized with a sudden idea.] Lundestad, here is the opportunity!
[Looks for his hat and slips quietly towards the door.
Yes, I will make a speech!
Fill your glasses, ladies and gentlemen! I am going to make a speech which shall begin with a fable; for here I seem to breathe the finer air of fable-land.
[The Chamberlain takes his glass from the card-table on the right, beside which he remains standing. Ringdal, Fieldbo, and one or two other gentlemen come in from the garden.

It was in the spring time. There came a young cuckoo flying over the uplands. Now the cuckoo is an adventurer. There was a great Bird-Parliament on the meadow beneath him, and both wild and tame fowl flocked to it. They came tripping out of the hen-yards; they waddled up from the goose-ponds; down, from Stonelee hulked a fat capercailzie, flying low and noisily; he settled down, and ruffled his feathers and flapped his wings, and made himself even broader than he was; and every now and then he crowed: “Krak, krak, krak!” as much as to say: I’m the game-cock from Stonelee, I am!

And then there was an old woodpecker. He bustled up and down the tree-trunks, pecking with his pointed beak, and gorging himself with grubs and everything that turns to gall. To right and left you heard him going: prik, prik, prik! And that was the woodpecker.
Excuse me, wasn’t it a stork, or a——?[16]

That was the old woodpecker. But now there came life into the crew; for they found something to cackle evil about. And they flustered together, and cackled in chorus, until at last the young cuckoo began to join in the cackling——
[Unnoticed.] For God’s sake, man, be quiet!

Now it was an eagle they cackled about—an eagle who dwelt in lonely dignity upon a beetling cliff.[17] They were all agreed about him. “He’s a bugbear to the neighbourhood,” croaked a hoarse raven. But the eagle swooped down into their midst, seized the cuckoo, and bore him aloft to his eyrie.—Heart conquered heart! From that clear summit the adventurer-cuckoo looked far and wide over the lowlands; there he found sunshine and peace; and there he learned to judge aright the swarm from the hen-yards and the clearings——
[Loudly.] Bravo, bravo! And now some music.
Chamberlain Bratsberg—here my fable ends; and here I stand before you, in the presence of every one, to beg your forgiveness for last night.

I thank you for the magnanimous vengeance you have taken for my senseless words. In me you have henceforth a faithful champion. And now, ladies and gentlemen, I drink the health of the eagle on the mountain-top—the health of Chamberlain Bratsberg.
[Clutching at the table.] Thank you, Mr.—Mr. Stensgård.
[For the most part in painful embarrassment.] The Chamberlain! Chamberlain Bratsberg!
Oh, Doctor, Doctor, what have you done?done?
[With his glass in his hand, radiant with self-satisfaction.] Now to our places again! Hullo, Fieldbo! Come, join in—join in the League of Youth! The game’s going merrily!
[In front, on the left.] Yes, on my soul, the game’s going merrily!
[Lundestad slips out by the door in the back.

14. An allusion to Holberg’s comedy, Jeppe på Bierget, which deals with the theme of Abou Hassan, treated by Shakespeare in the Induction to The Taming of the Shrew, and by Hauptmann in Schluck und Jau.
15. Pronounce “Shöblom”—the modified “ö” much as in German.
16. As before stated, “Heire” means a heron.
17. “Et brat fjeld”—an allusion to the name Bratsberg.

div.head: ACT THIRD.
div.p: An elegant morning-room, with entrance-door in the back. On the left, the door of the Chamberlain’s study; further back, a door leading to the drawing-room. On the right, a door leading to Ringdal’s offices; further forward, a window.
Thora is seated on the sofa, left, weeping. The Chamberlain paces angrily up and down.
Yes, now we have the epilogue—tears and lamentations——
Oh, that we had never seen that man!
That wretched Mr. Stensgård, of course.
You should rather say: Oh, that we had never seen that wretched Doctor.
Yes, Fieldbo, Fieldbo! Wasn’t it he that palmed off a parcel of lies upon me——?
No, my dear father, it was I.
You? Well, then, both of you! You were his accomplice—behind my back. A nice state of affairs!
Oh, father, if you only knew——
Oh, I know enough; more than enough; much more!
Dr. Fieldbo enters from the back.
Good morning, Chamberlain! Good morning, Miss Bratsberg!
[Still pacing the room.] So you are there, are you—bird of evil omen!
Yes, it was a very unpleasant affair.
[Looking out at the window.] Oh, you think so?
You must have noticed how I kept my eye upon Stensgård all the evening. Unfortunately, when I heard there was to be a game of forfeits, I thought there was no danger——
[Stamping on the floor.] To be made a laughing-stock by such a windbag! What must my guests have thought of me? That I was mean enough to want to buy this creature, this—this——as Lundestad calls him!
[After a short pause, turns to Fieldbo.] Tell me frankly, Doctor:—Am I really denser than the general run of people?
How can you ask such a question. Chamberlain?
Then how did it happen that I was probably the only person there who didn’t understand that that confounded speech was meant for me?
It is because you yourself regard your position in the district differently from other people.
I regard my position as my father before me regarded his. No one would ever have ventured to treat him so.
Your father died about the year 1830.

Oh, yes; many a barrier has broken down since that time. But, after all, it’s my own fault. I have mixed myself up too much with these good people. So now I must be content to have my name coupled with Anders Lundestad’s!
Well, frankly, I see no disgrace in that.

Oh, you know quite well what I mean. Of course I don’t plume myself on rank, or titles, or anything of that sort. But what I hold in honour, and expect others to hold in honour, is the integrity handed down in our family from generation to generation. What I mean is that when a man like Lundestad goes into public life, he cannot keep his character and his conduct entirely free from stain. In the general mud-throwing, he is sure to find himself bespattered. But they might leave me in peace; I stand outside their parties.
Not so entirely, Chamberlain; at least you were delighted so long as you thought it was Monsen that was attacked.
Don’t mention that fellow!—It is he that has relaxed the moral sense of the district. And now he has gone and turned my son’s head, confound him!
Yes; what tempted him to go and set up in business? It leads to nothing.
Why, my dear Chamberlain, he must live and——
Oh, with economy he could quite well live on the money that came to him from his mother.
He might perhaps live on it; but what could he live for?
For? Well, if he absolutely must have something to live for, hasn’t he qualified as a lawyer? He might live for his profession.

No, that he couldn’t do; it is against his nature. Then there was no official appointment he could well hope for; you have kept the management of your property in your own hands; and your son has no children to educate. Under these circumstances, when he sees tempting examples around him—people who have started from nothing and are worth their half million——

Their half million! Oh, come now, let us keep to the hundred thousands. But neither the half million nor the hundred thousands can be scraped together with perfectly clean hands;—I don’t mean in the eyes of the world; Heaven knows it is easy enough to keep within the law; but in respect to one’s own conscience. Of course my son cannot descend to anything questionable; so you may be quite sure Mr. Erik Bratsberg’s financial operations won’t bring in any half millions.
Selma, in walking dress, enters from the back.
Good-morning, child! Are you looking for your husband?
Yes, he said he was coming here. Mr. Monsen called upon him early this morning, and then——
Monsen? Does Monsen come to your house?
Now and then; generally on business. Why, my dear Thora, what’s the matter? Have you been crying?
No, it’s not nothing! At home Erik was out of humour, and here——I can see it in your looks: there is something wrong. What is it?

Nothing you need trouble about, at any rate. You are too dainty to carry burdens, my little Selma. Go into the drawing-room for the present. If Erik said he was coming, he will be here soon, no doubt.
Come, Thora—and be sure you don’t let me sit in a draught! [Embracing her.] Oh, I could hug the life out of you, my sweet Thora!
[The two ladies go off to the left.
So they are hand in glove, are they, the two speculators! They should go into partnership. Monsen and Bratsberg—how nice it would sound! [A knock at the door in the back.] Come in!
Yes, here I am again, Chamberlain!
You retired early yesterday evening. When Fieldbo had explained to me how matters stood, you had already——
I understand that; therefore I have not come to make any.
I know I have insulted you.
I know that too; and before I have you turned out, perhaps you will be good enough to tell me why you are here.
Because I love your daughter, Chamberlain!
Ah, you can’t grasp the idea, Chamberlain. You are an old man; you have nothing to fight for——
I am here to ask for your daughter’s hand, Chamberlain.
What do you say to this. Doctor?
Oh, Fieldbo is on my side; he is my friend; the only true friend I have.
No, no, man! Never in this world, if you——
Perhaps it was with this view that Doctor Fieldbo secured his friend’s introduction into my house?

You know me only by my exploits of yesterday and the day before. That is not enough. Besides, I am not the same man to-day that I was then. My intercourse with you and yours has fallen like spring showers upon my spirit, making it put forth new blossoms in a single night! You must not hurl me back into my sordid past. Till now, I have never been at home with the beautiful in life; it has always been beyond my reach——

Yes, for I have will on my side. Remember what you told me yesterday. You were opposed to your son’s marriage—and see how it has turned out! You must put on the glasses of experience, as Fieldbo said——
Ah, that was what you meant?
Not in the least! My dear Chamberlain, let me speak to him alone——
Nonsense; I have nothing to speak to you about. Now, pray be reasonable, Chamberlain! A family like yours needs new alliances, or its brains stagnate——

Now, now, don’t get angry! These high-and-mighty airs are unworthy of you—of course you know they are all nonsense at bottom. You shall see how much you’ll value me when you come to know me. Yes, yes; you shall value me—both you and your daughter! I will make her——
What do you think of this, Doctor?
Yes, it would be in you; but I, you see—I have a mission to fulfil on God’s beautiful earth;—I am not to be deterred by nonsensical prejudices.prejudices.
Mr. Stensgård, there is the door.
Out with you! You are an adventurer,adventurer, an a—a—confound my memory! You’re a——
You are—that other thing—it’s on the tip of my tongue——
Beware how you block my career!

I will attack you in the papers, persecute you, libel you, do all I can to undermine your reputation. You shall shriek under the lash. You shall seem to see spirits in the air raining blows upon you. You shall huddle together in dread, and crouch with your arms bent over your head to ward off the strokes—you shall try to creep into shelter——
Creep into shelter yourself—in a madhouse; that is the proper place for you!

Ha-ha; that is a cheap retort; but you know no better, Mr. Bratsberg! I tell you the wrath of the Lord is in me. It is His will you are opposing. He has destined me for the light—beware how you cast a shadow!—Well, I see I shall make no way with you to-day; but that matters nothing. I only ask you to speak to your daughter—to prepare her—to give her the opportunity of choosing! Reflect, and look around you. Where can you expect to find a son-in-law among these plodding dunces? Fieldbo says she is deep and steadfast and true. So now you know just how matters stand. Good-bye, Chamberlain—I leave you to choose between my friendship and my enmity. Good-bye!
So it has come to this! This is how they dare to treat me in my own house!
Stensgård dares; no one else would.
Let them come; I shall keep them off; I would go through fire and water for you——!
Yes, you who have caused all the mischief!—H’m; that Stensgård is the most impudent scoundrel I have ever known! And yet, after all—deuce take me if there isn’t something I like about him.
He has openness, Dr Fieldbo! He doesn’t go playing his own game behind one’s back, like so many other people; he—he——!
It’s not worth disputing about. Only be firm, Chamberlain; no, and no again, to Stensgård——!
Oh, keep your advice to yourself! You may rely upon it that neither he nor any one else——
[Enters by the door on the right.] Excuse me, Chamberlain; one word——
He came in by the back way, and begs you to see him.

H’m.—Oh, Doctor, just go into the drawing-room for a moment; there’s some one here who——But don’t say a word to Selma of Mr. Stensgård and his visit. She must be kept outside all this business. As for my daughter, I should prefer that you should say nothing to her either; but——Oh, what’s the use——? Please go now.
[Fieldbo goes into the drawing-room. Ringdal has, in the meantime, gone back to his office, whence Monsen presently enters.
[At the door.] I beg ten thousand pardons, sir——
I trust your family is in good health?
Thank you. Is there anything you want?
I can’t quite put it that way. Thank heaven, I’m one of those that have got pretty nearly all they can want.
Oh, indeed? That is a good deal to say.
But I’ve had to work for it, Chamberlain. Oh, I know you regard my work with no very friendly eye.
I cannot suppose that your work is in any way affected by my way of regarding it.
Who knows? At any rate, I’m thinking of gradually withdrawing from business.
The luck has been on my side, I may tell you. I’ve gone ahead as far as I care to; so now I think it’s about time to slack off a little——
Well, I congratulate both you—and other people.
And if I could at the same time do you a service, Chamberlain——
When the Langerud woods were put up to auction five years ago, you made a bid for them——
Yes, but you outbade me, and they were knocked down to you.
You can have them now, with the saw-mills and all appurtenances——
After all your sinful cutting and hacking——!
Oh, they’re worth a good deal still; and with your method of working, in a few years——
Thank you; unfortunately I must decline the proposal.
There’s a great deal of money in it, Chamberlain. As for me,—I may tell you I have a great speculation on hand; the stakes are large; I mean there’s a big haul to be made—a hundred thousand or so——
A hundred thousand? That is certainly no trifle.

Ha ha ha! A nice round sum to add to the pile. But when you’re going into a great battle you need reserve forces, as the saying goes. There’s not much ready money about; the names that are worth anything are rather used up——
Yes, certain people have taken care of that.
It’s a case of you scratch me, I scratch you. Well, Chamberlain, is it to be a bargain? You shall have the woods at your own figure——
I will not have them at any figure, Mr. Monsen.
Well, one good offer deserves another. Will you help me, sir?
Of course I’ll give good security. I have plenty of property. Look here—these papers—just let me explain my position to you.
[Waving the papers aside.] Is it pecuniary aid you want?
Not ready money; oh, no! But your support, Chamberlain. Of course I’ll pay for it—and give security, and——
And you come to me with such a proposal as this?
Yes, precisely to you. I know you’ve often let bygones be bygones when a man was in real straits.
Well, in a way, I must thank you for your good opinion—especially at a time like this; but nevertheless——
Won’t you tell me, Chamberlain, what sets you against me?
Oh, what would be the use?
It might lead to a better understanding between us. I’ve never stood in your way that I know of.

You think not? Then let me tell you of one case in which you have stood in my way. I founded the Iron-works Savings Bank for the benefit of my employees and others. But then you must needs set up as a banker; people take their savings to you——
Naturally, sir, for I give higher interest.
Yes, but you charge higher interest on loans.loans.
But I don’t make so many difficulties about security and so forth.

That is just the mischief of it; for now we have people making bargains to the tune of ten or twenty thousand dollars,[18] though neither of the parties has so much as a brass farthing. That is what sets me against you, Mr. Monsen. And there is another thing too that touches me still more nearly. Do you think it was with my good will that my son flung himself into all these wild speculations?
But how can I help that?
It was your example that infected him, as it did the others. Why could you not stick to your last?
Remain a lumberman, like my father?
Was it a disgrace to be in my employment? Your father made his bread honourably, and was respected in his own class.

Yes, until he’d almost worked his life out, and at last went over the waterfall with his raft. Do you know anything of life in that class, Chamberlain? Have you ever realised what the men have to endure who toil for you deep in the forests, and along the river-reaches, while you sit comfortably at home and fatten on the profits? Can you blame such a man for struggling to rise in the world? I had had a little more schooling than my father; perhaps I had rather more brains too——

Very likely. But by what means have you risen in the world? You began by selling brandy. Then you bought up doubtful debts, and enforced them mercilessly;—and so you got on and on. How many people have you not ruined to push yourself forward!
That’s the course of business; one up, another down.
But there are different methods of business. I know of respectable families whom you have brought to the workhouse.
Daniel Heire is not very far from the workhouse.

I understand you; but I can justify my conduct before God and man! When the country was in distress, after the separation from Denmark, my father made sacrifices beyond his means. Thus part of our property came into the hands of the Heire family. What was the result? The people who lived upon the property suffered under Daniel Heire’s incompetent management. He cut down timber to the injury, I may even say to the ruin, of the district. Was it not my obvious duty to put a stop to it if I was able? And it happened that I was able; I had the law on my side; I was well within my rights when I re-entered upon my family property.
I, too, have always had the law on my side.

But what about your sense of right, your conscience, if you have such a thing? And how you have broken down all social order! How you have impaired the respect that should attach to wealth! People never think of asking nowadays how such and such a fortune was made, or how long it has been in such and such a family; they only ask: how much is so-and-so worth?—and they esteem him accordingly. Now I suffer by all this; I find myself regarded as a sort of associate of yours; people speak of us in one breath, because we are the two largest proprietors in the neighbourhood. This state of things I cannot endure! I tell you once for all: that is why I am set against you.
This state of things shall come to an end, sir; I will give up business, and make way for you at every point; but I beg you, I implore you, to help me!
I’m willing to pay what you like——
To pay! And you dare to——!
If not for my sake, then for your son’s!
Yes, he’s in it. I reckon he stands to win some twenty thousand dollars.
Then, good God, who stands to lose all this money?
If my son wins, some one or other must lose!
It’s a good stroke of business; I’m not in a position to say more. But I need a solid name; only just your endorsement——
Only for ten or fifteen thousand dollars.
Do you suppose for a moment that——? My name! In such an affair! My name? As surety, no doubt?
A matter of swindling! My name! Not upon any consideration. I have never put my name on other men’s paper.
No, not literal; I’ve seen it with my own eyes.
Your name—on one bill at least.
It is false, I tell you! You have never seen it!
I have! On a bill for two thousand dollars. Think again!
Neither for two thousand nor for ten thousand! On my sacred word of honour, never!
Yes, a forgery—for I have seen it.
Forgery? Forgery! Where did you see it? In whose hands?
Ha-ha! We shall soon find that out.out.
Silence! It has come to this then! Forgery. They must mix me up in their abominations! No wonder, then, that people bracket me with the rest of you. But it is my turn now!
Chamberlain—for your own sake and for the sake of others——

Off with you! Out of my sight! It is you that are at the root of it all!—Yes you are! Woe unto him from whom offences come. Your home-life is scandalous. What sort of society do you get about you? Persons from Christiania and elsewhere, who think only of eating and drinking, and do not care in what company they gorge themselves. Silence! I have seen with my own eyes your distinguished guests tearing along the roads at Christmas-time like a pack of howling wolves. And there is worse behind. You have had scandals with your own maid-servants. You drove your wife out of her mind by your ill-treatment and debauchery.
Come, this is going too far! You shall pay for these words!
Oh, to the deuce with your threats! What harm can you do to me? Me? You asked what I had to say against you. Well, I have said it. Now you know why I have kept you out of decent society.
Yes, and now I’ll drag your decent society down——
[Opens the door on the right and calls.] Ringdal, Ringdal—come here!
[Calls into the drawing-room.] Doctor, please come this way!—Now, Ringdal, now you shall see my prophecies fulfilled.
[Entering.] What can I do for you, Chamberlain?
What do you say to this, Doctor? You have always accused me of exaggerating when I said that Monsen was corrupting the neighbourhood.
We are getting on, I can tell you! What do you think? There are forgeries going about.
Yes, forgeries! And whose name do you think they have forged? Why, mine!
Who in the world can have done it?

How can I tell? I don’t know all the scoundrels in the district. But we shall soon find out.—Doctor, do me a service. The papers must have come into the hands either of the Savings Bank or the Iron-works Bank. Drive up to Lundestad; he is the director who knows most about things. Find out whether there is any such paper——
Lundestad is here at the works to-day; there’s a meeting of the school committee.
So much the better. Find him; bring him here.
And you, Ringdal, make inquiries at the Ironworks. As soon as we have got to the bottom of the matter, we’ll lay an information. No mercy to the scoundrels!
Very good, sir. Bless me, who’d have thought of such a thing?
[The Chamberlain paces the room once or twice, and is then about to go into his study. At that instant Erik Bratsberg enters from the back.
I want so much to speak to you.
H’m; I’m not much in the humour for speaking to any one. What do you want?
You know I have never mixed you up in my affairs, father.
No; that is an honour I should certainly have declined.
But now I am forced to——
What are you forced to do?
With money! You may be very sure that——
Only this once! I swear I’ll never again——The fact is, I am under certain engagements to Monsen of Stonelee——
I know that. You have a brilliant speculation on hand.
A speculation? We? No! Who told you so?
He has just gone. I showed him the door.
If you don’t help me, father, I am ruined.
Yes. Monsen has advanced me money. I had to pay terribly dear for it; and now the bills have fallen due——
There we have it! What did I tell you——?
Yes, yes; it’s too late now——

Ruined! In two years! But how could you expect anything else? What had you to do among these charlatans that go about dazzling people’s eyes with wealth that never existed! They were no company for you. Among people of that sort you must meet cunning with cunning, or you’ll go to the wall; you have learnt that now.
Father, will you save me or will you not?
No; for the last time, no. I will not.

Oh, let us have no big phrases! There’s no honour involved in commercial success nowadays; quite the opposite, I had almost said. Go home and make up your accounts; pay every man his due, and have done with it, the sooner the better.
Selma and Thora enter from the drawing-room.
Is that Erik’s voice?—Good heavens, what is the matter?
Nothing. Go into the drawing-room again.
No, I won’t go. I will know. Erik, what is it? Tell me!
It’s only that I am ruined!
Do you mean you have lost your money?
Is that what you call everything?
Come, let us go, Selma. You are all I have left me. We must bear the blow together.
The blow? Bear it together? [With a cry.] Do you think I am fit for that, now?
No, I won’t take care! I cannot go on lying and shamming any longer! I must speak the truth. I will not “bear” anything!

Oh, how cruel you have been to me! Shamefully—all of you! It was my part always to accept—never to give. I have been like a pauper among you. You never came and demanded a sacrifice of me; I was not fit to bear anything. I hate you! I loathe you!
She is ill; she is out of her mind!

How I have thirsted for a single drop of your troubles, your anxieties! But when I begged for it you only laughed me off. You have dressed me up like a doll; you have played with me as you would play with a child. Oh, what a joy it would have been to me to take my share in your burdens! How I longed, how I yearned, for a large, and high, and strenuous part in life! Now you come to me, Erik, now that you have nothing else left. But I will not be treated simply as a last resource. I will have nothing to do with your troubles now. I won’t stay with you! I will rather play and sing in the streets——! Let me be! Let me be!
Thora, was there any meaning in all that, or——
Oh, yes, there was meaning in it; if only I had seen it sooner.
No! All else I can lose, but not her! Selma, Selma!
I have been to the Bank——
The Bank? Oh, yes, about the bill——
It’s all right; they have never had any bill endorsed by you——
Fieldbo and Lundestad enter by the back.
Indeed? Not at the Savings Bank either?
Certainly not. During all the years I’ve been a director I have never once seen your name; except, of course, on your son’s bill.
Yes, the bill you accepted for him early this spring.
My son? My son? Do you dare to tell me——?
Why, bless me, just think a moment; the bill for two thousand dollars drawn by your son——
[Groping for a chair.] Oh, my God——!
[Who has sunk down on a chair.] Quietly, quietly! Drawn by my son, you say? Accepted by me? For two thousand dollars?
[To Lundestad.] And this bill is in the Savings Bank?
Not now; it was redeemed last week by Monsen——
Monsen may still be at the works; I’ll go——
Daniel Heire enters by the back.
Good-morning, gentlemen! Good-morning, Chamberlain! Thank you so much for the delightful evening we spent yesterday. What do you think I’ve just heard——?
So are other people, I can tell you; our friend from Stonelee, for example——
Hee-hee; it’s a pretty story! The electioneering intrigues are in full swing. And what do you think is the last idea? They are going to bribe you, Chamberlain!
They judge the tree by its fruit.

Deuce take me if it isn’t the most impudent thing I ever heard of! I just looked in at Madam Rundholmen’s to have a glass of bitters. There sat Messrs. Monsen and Stensgård drinking port—filthy stuff! I wouldn’t touch it; but they might have had the decency to offer me a glass, all the same. However, Monsen turned to me and said, “What do you bet that Chamberlain Bratsberg won’t go with our party at the preliminary election to-morrow?” “Indeed,” said I, “how’s that to be managed?” “Oh,” he said, “this bill will persuade him——”
Oh, I know no more. They said something about two thousand dollars. That’s the figure they rate a gentleman’s conscience at! Oh, it’s abominable, I say!
A bill for two thousand dollars?
No, he handed it over to Stensgård.
Quite certain. “You can make what use you please of it,” he said. But I don’t understand——
I want to speak to you, Mr. Heire—and you too, Ringdal.
[The three converse in a whisper at the back.
Your son’s bill is genuine, of course——?
Of course. But now if the forged bill were to turn up——?
Naturally not;—but you must do more.
Yes, for heaven’s sake, you can and must. You must save the poor fellow——
Quite simply: by acknowledging the signature.
Then you think, Doctor, that we stick at nothing in our family?
I am trying to think for the best, Chamberlain.
And do you believe for a moment that I can tell a lie?—that I can play into the hands of forgers?
And do you realise what will be the consequences if you do not?
The offender must settle that with the law.

div.head: ACT FOURTH.
div.p: A public room in Madam Rundholmen’s hotel. Entrance door in the back; a smaller door on either side. A window on the right; before it, a table with writing materials; further back, in the middle of the room, another table.
[Within, on the left, heard talking loudly.] Oh, let them go about their business! Tell them they’ve come here to vote and not to drink. If they won’t wait, they can do the other thing.
[Enters by the back.] Good-morning! H’m, h’m, Madam Rundholmen! [Goes to the door on the left and knocks.] Good-morning, Madam Rundholmen!
It is I—Stensgård. May I come in?
No, indeed you mustn’t! No! I’m not dress’d.
What? Are you so late to-day?

Oh, I can tell you I’ve been up since all hours; but one must look a little decent, you know. [Peeps out, with a kerchief over her head.] Well, what is it? No, you really mustn’t look at me, Mr. Stensgård.—Oh, there’s some one else!
[Enters from the back with a bundle of papers.] Good morning, Mr. Stensgård.
Yes, here it is. Look—“The Independence Day Celebrations—From our Special Correspondent.” Here’s the founding of the League on the other side, and your speech up here. I’ve leaded all the abuse.
It seems to me it’s all leaded.
And the extra number was of course distributed yesterday?
Of course; all over the district, both to subscribers and others. Would you like to see it?

[Running his eye over the paper.] “Our respected member, Mr. Lundestad, proposes to resign ... long and faithful service ... in the words of the poet: 'Rest, patriot, it is thy due!'” H’m! “The association founded on Independence Day: the League of Youth ... Mr. Stensgård, the guiding intelligence of the League ... timely reforms, credit on easier terms.” Ah, that’s very good. Has the polling begun?
It’s in full swing. The whole League is on the spot—both voters and others.
Oh, deuce take the others—between ourselves, of course. Well, you go down and talk to the waverers.
You can tell them that I am pretty much at one with Lundestad——
Trust to me; I know the local situation.
One thing more; just to oblige me, Aslaksen, don’t drink to-day.
We’ll have a jolly evening when it’s all over; but remember what you, as well as I, have at stake; your paper——Come, now, my good fellow, let me see that you can——
There, that’s enough now; I’m old enough to look after myself.
[Enters from the left, elaborately dressed.] Now, Mr. Stensgård, I’m at your service. Is it anything of importance——?
No, only that I want you to be good enough to let me know when Mr. Monsen comes.
No; he drove past here at four this morning; he’s always driving about nowadays. What’s more, he came in and roused me out of bed—he wanted to borrow money, you must know.
Yes. He’s a tremendous man to get through money is Monsen. I hope things may turn out all right for him. And I say the same to you; for I hear you’re going into Parliament.
I? Nonsense. Who told you so?
Oh, some of Mr. Lundestad’s people.
[Enters from the back.] Hee-hee! Good-morning! I’m not in the way, am I?
Good God, how resplendent! Can it be for me that you’ve got yourself up like this?
Of course. It’s for you bachelors we get ourselves up, isn’t it?
For marrying men, Madam Rundholmen; for marrying men! Unfortunately, my law-suits take up all my time——
Oh, nonsense; you’ve always plenty of time to get married.
No; deuce take me if I have! Marriage is a thing you’ve got to give your whole mind to. Well, well—if you can’t have me, you must put up with somebody else. For you ought to marry again.
Now, do you know, I’m sometimes of the same opinion.
Naturally; when once one has tasted the joys of matrimony——Of course, poor Rundholmen was one in a thousand——
Well, I won’t go so far as that; he was a bit rough, and rather too fond of his glass; but a husband’s always a husband.
Very true, Madam Rundholmen; a husband’s a husband, and a widow’s a widow——

And business is business. Oh, when I think of all I’ve got to attend to, I don’t know whether I’m on my heels or my head. Every one wants to buy; but when it comes to paying, I’ve got to go in for summonses and executions, and Lord knows what. Upon my word, I’ll soon have to engage a lawyer all to myself.
I’ll tell you what, Madam Rundholmen, you should retain Mr. Stensgård; he’s a bachelor.
Oh, how you do talk! I won’t listen to a word more.
A substantial woman, sir! Comfortable and well-preserved; no children up to date; money well invested. Education too; she’s widely read, sir.
Hee-hee; she ought to be; she had charge of Alm’s circulating library for a couple of years. But your head’s full of other things to-day, I daresay.
Not at all; I don’t even know that I shall vote. Who are you going to vote for, Mr. Heire?
Haven’t got a vote, sir. There was only one kennel that would qualify in the market, and that you bought.
If you’re at a loss for a lodging, I’ll give it up to you.

Hee-hee, you’re joking. Ah, youth, youth! What a pleasant humour it has! But now I must be off and have a look at the menagerie. I’m told your whole League is afoot. [Sees Fieldbo, who enters from the back.] Here’s the Doctor too! I suppose you have come on a scientific mission?
Yes, to study the epidemic; you’ve heard of the virulent rabies agitatoria that has broken out? God be with you, my dear young friends?
Tell me quickly—have you seen the Chamberlain to-day?
Yes; you know I have written to him.
Have you? What did you write?
That I am still of the same mind about his daughter; that I want to talk the matter over with him; and that I propose to call on him to-morrow.
If I were you, I should at least defer my visit. It is the Chamberlain’s birthday to-morrow; a crowd of people will be there——
That’s all right; the more the better. I hold big cards in my hand, let me tell you.
And perhaps you have bluffed a little with your big cards?
I mean you have perhaps embellished your declaration of love with a few little threats or so?
Fieldbo, you have seen the letter!
Well then, frankly—I have threatened him.
Ah! Then I have, in a way, an answer to your letter.
An answer? Out with it, man!
[Shows him a sealed paper.] Look here—the Chamberlain’s proxy.
And who does he vote for?
Not for you, at any rate.
For the Sheriff and the Provost.[19]
No. And do you know why? Because Lundestad is going to propose you as his successor.
Yes, he does. And he added: “If you see Stensgård, you can tell him how I am voting; it will show him on what footing we stand.”
Good; since he will have it so!
Take care; it’s dangerous to tug at an old tower—it may come down on your head.
Oh, I have learnt wisdom in these two days.
Indeed? You’re not so wise but that you let old Lundestad lead you by the nose.

Do you think I haven’t seen through Lundestad? Do you think I don’t understand that he took me up because he thought I had won over the Chamberlain, and because he wanted to break up our League and keep Monsen out?
But now that he knows you haven’t won over the Chamberlain——
He has gone too far to draw back; and I’ve made good use of the time, and scattered announcements broadcast. Most of his supporters will abstain from voting; mine are all here——
It’s a big stride from the preliminary election to the final election.
Lundestad knows very well that if he fails me in the College of Electors, I’ll soon agitate him out of the Town Council.
Not a bad calculation. And to succeed in all this, you feel that you must strike root here more firmly than you have as yet done?
Yes, these people always demand material guarantees, community of interests——
Just so; and therefore Miss Bratsberg is to be sacrificed?

Sacrificed? If that were so, I should be no better than a scoundrel. But it will be for her happiness, that I’m convinced. What now? Fieldbo, why do you look like that? You have some underhand scheme of your own——
Yes, you have! You are intriguing against me, behind my back. Why do you do that? Be open with me—will you?

Frankly, I won’t. You are so dangerous, so unscrupulous—well, so reckless at any rate, that one dare not be open with you. Whatever you know, you make use of without hesitation. But this I say to you as a friend: put Miss Bratsberg out of your head.

I cannot. I must extricate myself from these sordid surroundings. I can’t go on living in this hugger-mugger way. Here have I got to be hail-fellow-well-met with Dick, Tom, and Harry; to whisper in corners with them, to hob-nob with them, to laugh at their beery witticisms; to be hand in glove with hobbledehoys and unlicked cubs. How can I keep my love of the People untarnished in the midst of all this? I feel as if all the electricity went out of my words. I have no elbow-room, no fresh air to breathe. Oh, a longing comes over me at times for exquisite women! I want something that brings beauty with it! I lie here in a sort of turbid eddy, while out there the clear blue current sweeps past me——But what can you understand of all this!
[Enters from the back.] Ah, here we are. Good-morning, gentlemen.
I have news for you, Mr. Lundestad! Do you know who the Chamberlain is voting for?
What do I care? He is voting for the Sheriff and the Provost.
Oh, that was to be expected. You went and ruined your chances with him—though I implored you to play your cards neatly.
I shall play them neatly enough—in future.
Take care—two can play at that game.
That fellow has something up his sleeve. Have you any idea what it can be?
No, I haven’t. But, by-the-bye, I see you are flourishing in the paper to-day.
Yes, with a nice little epitaph on me.
Oh, that’s that beast Aslaksen, of course——
Your attack on the Chamberlain is in too.
I don’t know anything about that. If it’s to be war between the Chamberlain and me, I have sharper weapons.
Have you ever seen this bill? Look at it. Is it good?
Good, you say? This bill here?

[Enters from the right.] Why, what the deuce can be the meaning of——Ah, how interesting! Do remain as you are, gentlemen, I beg! Do you know what you irresistibly remind me of? Of a summer night in the Far North.

A very obvious one—the setting and the rising sun together. Delightful, delightful! But, talking of that, what the deuce is the matter outside there? Your fellow citizens are scuttling about like frightened fowls, cackling and crowing and not knowing what perch to settle on.
Well, it’s an occasion of great importance.
Oh, you and your importance! No, it’s something quite different, my dear friends. There are whispers of a great failure; a bankruptcy—oh, not political, Mr. Lundestad; I don’t mean that!

Hee-hee! That puts life into our legal friend. Yes, a bankruptcy; some one is on his last legs; the axe is laid to the root of the tree——I say no more! Two strange gentlemen have been seen driving past; but where to? To whose address? Do you know anything, Mr. Lundestad?
I know how to hold my tongue, Mr. Heire.

Of course; you are a statesman, a diplomatist. But I must be off and find out all I can about it. It’s such sport with these heroes of finance: they are like beads on a string—when one slips off, all the rest follow.
Is there any truth in all this gossip?
You showed me a bill; I thought I saw young Mr. Bratsberg’s name upon it?
And you asked me if it was good?
It’s perhaps not so good as it might be.
A forgery? Forged bills are often the safest; people redeem them first.
But what do you think? Isn’t it a forgery?
I don’t much like the look of it.
I’m afraid there are too many of these about, Mr. Stensgård.
If young Mr. Bratsberg slips off the string, those nearest him are only too likely to follow.
[Seizes his arm.] What do you mean by those nearest him?
Who can be nearer than father and son?
Remember, I say nothing! It was Daniel Heire that was talking of failure and bankruptcy and——
This is a thunderbolt to me.

Oh, many a man that seemed solid enough has gone to the wall before now. Perhaps he’s too good-natured; goes and backs bills; ready money isn’t always to be had; property has to be sold for an old song——
And of course this falls on—falls on the children as well.
Yes, I’m heartily grieved for Miss Bratsberg. She didn’t get much from her mother; and heaven knows if even the little she has is secured.
Oh, now I understand Fieldbo’s advice! He’s a true friend, after all.
He was too loyal to say anything, but I understand him all the same. And now I understand you too, Mr. Lundestad.
Have you not understood me before?
Not thoroughly. I forgot the proverb about the rats and the sinking ship.
That’s not a very nice way to put it. But what’s the matter with you? You look quite ill. Good God, I haven’t gone and blasted your hopes, have I?
Yes, yes—I see it all. Old fool that I am! My dear Mr. Stensgård, if you really love the girl, what does it matter whether she is rich or poor?
Good Lord, we all know happiness isn’t a matter of money.

And with industry and determination you’ll soon be on your feet again. Don’t let poverty frighten you. I know what love is; I went into all that in my young days. A happy home; a faithful woman——! My dear young friend, beware how you take any step that may involve you in life-long self-reproach.
But what will become of your plans?
Oh, they must go as best they can. I couldn’t think of demanding the sacrifice of your heart!

But I will make the sacrifice. Yes, I will show you that I have the strength for it. Think of the longing multitude out there: they claim me with a sort of voiceless pathos. I cannot, I dare not, fail them!
Yes, but the stake in the district——?

I shall take measures to fulfil the demands of my fellow citizens in that respect, Mr. Lundestad. I see a way, a new way; and I will follow it up. I renounce the happiness of toiling in obscurity for the woman I love. I say to my fellow countrymen: “Here I am—take me!”
[Looks at him in quiet admiration and presses his hand.] You are indeed a man of rare gifts, Mr. Stensgård.
[Stensgård paces the room several times, now stopping for a moment at the window, now running his fingers through his hair. Presently Bastian Monsen enters from the back.
Here I am, my dear friend.[20]
The Nation? What does that mean?
Don’t you know what the Nation means? It means the People; the common people; those who have nothing, and are nothing; those who lie chained——
What monkey-tricks are these, I should like to know?
I have noticed lately that you go about mimicking me; you imitate even my clothes and my handwriting. Be kind enough to stop that.
What do you mean? Don’t we belong to the same party?
Yes, but I won’t put up with this—you make yourself ridiculous——
By aping me. Be sensible now, Monsen, and give it up. It’s quite disgusting. But look here—can you tell me when your father is coming back?
I have no idea. I believe he’s gone to Christiania; he may not be back for a week or so.
Indeed? I’m sorry for that. He has a big stroke of business on hand, I hear.
I have a big stroke of business on hand too. Look here, Stensgård, you must do me a service.
I feel so full of energy. I have to thank you for that; you have stimulated me. I feel I must do something, Stensgård:—I want to get married.
Sh! Some one in this house.

Sh! Yes, it’s her. Put in a good word for me, do! This sort of thing is just the thing for me. She’s in the swim, you know; she’s on the best of terms with the Chamberlain’s people, ever since her sister was housekeeper there. If I get her, perhaps I shall get the town-contracts too. So that on the whole—damn it, I love her!
Oh, love, love! Have done with that sickening hypocrisy.

Yes; you are lying to yourself, at any rate. You talk in one breath of town-contracts and of love. Why not call a spade a spade? There’s something sordid about all this; I will have nothing to do with it.
Do your dirty work yourself, I say! [To Fieldbo, who enters from the right.] Well, how goes the election?
Excellently for you, it appears. I saw Lundestad just now; he said you were getting all the votes.
But what good will they do you? Since you’re not a man of property——
Well, you can’t do two things at once. If you win on the one side, you must be content to lose on the other. Good-bye!
What did he mean by winning and losing?
I’ll tell you afterwards. But now, my dear Monsen—to return to what we were talking about—I promised to put in a good word for you——
You promised? On the contrary, I thought you said——?

Oh, nonsense; you didn’t let me explain myself fully. What I meant was that there is something sordid in mixing up your love with town-contracts and so forth; it is an offence against all that is noblest in your nature. So, my dear friend, if you really love the girl——
Yes, yes; it’s all the same. I mean when one really loves a woman, that in itself should be a conclusive reason——
Yes, that’s just what I think. So you’ll speak for me, will you?
Yes, with great pleasure—but on one condition.
Tit for tat, my dear Bastian—you must put in a word for me too.
Have you really not noticed anything? Yet it’s before your very nose.
Your sister Ragna? Yes, it is she. Oh, you don’t know how I have been moved by the sight of her quiet, self-sacrificing devotion to her home——
Do you really mean to say so?
And you, with your penetrating eye, have suspected nothing?
Yes, at one time I did think——; but now people are talking of your hanging about the Chamberlain’s——
Oh, the Chamberlain’s! Well, Monsen, I’ll tell you frankly that for a moment I did hesitate; but, thank goodness, that is over; now I see my way quite clear before me.
There’s my hand. I’ll back you up, you may be sure. And as for Ragna—why, she daren’t do anything but what I and father wish.
Yes, but your father—that’s just what I wanted to say——

Sh! There—I hear Madam Rundholmen. Now’s your chance to speak for me, if she’s not too busy; for then she’s apt to be snappish. You do your best, my dear fellow, and leave the rest to me. Do you happen to have seen Aslaksen?
[Bastian goes out by the back, as Madam Rundholmen enters from the right.
Things are going as smooth as possible, Mr. Stensgård; every one is voting for you.
Goodness knows what Monsen of Stonelee will say.
I want a word with you, Madam Rundholmen.
Well then: you were talking just now about being alone in the world——
Oh, it was that horrid old Heire——
You were saying how hard it is for an unprotected widow——
Yes, indeed; you should just try it, Mr. Stensgård!
But now if there came a fine young man——
One who had long loved you in secret——
Oh, come now, Mr. Stensgård, I won’t hear any more of your nonsense.
You must! A young man who, like yourself, finds it hard to be alone in the world——
Well, what then? I don’t understand you at all.
If you could make two people happy, Madam Rundholmen—yourself and——
Mr. Stensgård, you can’t be in earnest?
You don’t suppose I would jest on such a subject? Should you be disposed——?
Yes, that I am, the Lord knows! Oh, you dear, sweet——
Ragna Monsen enters hastily, and in evident disquietude, from the back.
I beg your pardon—isn’t my father here?
Your father? Yes; no;—I—I don’t know—excuse me——
Your father? Oh, he drove past here——
Yes, I know for certain he drove down the road. Oh, my dear Miss Monsen, you can’t think how happy I am! Wait a moment—I’ll just run to the cellar, and fetch up a bottle of the real thing.
Tell me, Miss Monsen—is it really your father you are looking for?
And you didn’t know that he had gone away?
Oh, how should I know? They tell me nothing. But to Christiania——? That’s impossible; they would have met him. Good-bye!
[Intercepts her.] Ragna! Tell me! Why are you so changed towards me?
I? Let me pass! Let me go!
No, you shall not go! I believe Providence guided you here at this moment. Oh, why do you shrink from me? You used not to.
Ah, that is all over, thank God!
I have learnt to know you better; it is well that I learned in time.

Oh, that is it? People have been lying about me? Perhaps I am to blame too; I have been lost in a maze of perplexities. But that is past now. Oh, the very sight of you makes a better man of me. It is you I care for, deeply and truly; it is you I love, Ragna—you and no other!
Let me pass! I am afraid of you——
Oh, but to-morrow, Ragna—may I come and speak to you to-morrow?
Yes, yes, if you must; only for heaven’s sake not to-day.
Only not to-day! Hurrah! I have won; now I am happy!
[Enters from the left with cake and wine.] Come now, we must drink a glass for luck.
For luck in love! Here’s to love and happiness! Hurrah for to-morrow!
[Entering from the right, to Ragna.] Have you found him?
No, he is not here. Come, come!
Heaven help us, what’s the matter?
Nothing; only some visitors have arrived at Stonelee——
Thanks for all your kindness, Madam Rundholmen——
Oh, have you got visitors on your hands again?
Yes, yes; excuse me; I must go home. Good-bye!
[Ragna and Helle go out by the back.
Daniel Heire enters from the right.
Ha-ha! It’s going like a house on fire! They’re all cackling Stensgård, Stensgård, Stensgård! They’re all plumping for you. Now you should plump for him too, Madam Rundholmen!
Hey, that’s an idea! Are they all voting for him?
Unanimously—Mr. Stensgård enjoys the confidence of the constituency, as the saying is. Old Lundestad is going about with a face like a pickled cucumber. Oh, it’s a pleasure to see it all.
They shan’t regret having voted for him. If I can’t vote, I can stand treat.
Ah, you are the man for the widows, Mr. Stensgård! I’ll tell you what—if you can only get hold of her, you’re a made man, sir!
Yes, why not? She’s a substantial woman in every sense of the word. She’ll be mistress of the situation as soon as the Stonelee card-castle has come to grief.
There’s nothing wrong at Stonelee, is there?
Isn’t there? You have a short memory, my dear sir. Didn’t I tell you there were rumours of failure, and bankruptcy, and——?
What then? That’s just what we want to know. There’s a hue and cry after Monsen; two men have come to Stonelee——
Yes, I know—a couple of visitors——

Uninvited visitors, my dear young friend; there are whispers of the police and infuriated creditors—there’s something queer about the accounts, you must know! Talking of that—what paper was that Monsen gave you yesterday?
Oh, just a paper——Something queer about the accounts, you say? Look here! you know Chamberlain Bratsberg’s signature?
Hee-hee! I should rather think I did.
[Produces the bill.] Well, look at this.
Give it here—I’m rather short-sighted, you know. [After examining it.] That, my dear sir? That’s not the Chamberlain’s hand.
Nonsense! Let me see. [Looks at the paper and hands it back again.] You can light your cigar with this.
A forgery, young man; a forgery, as sure as my name’s Daniel. You have only to look at it with the keen eye of suspicion——
But how can that be? Monsen can’t have known——

Monsen? No, he knows nothing about either his own paper or other people’s. But I’m glad it has come to an end, Mr. Stensgård!—It’s a satisfaction to one’s moral sense. Ah, I have often glowed with a noble indignation, if I may say so, at having to stand by and see——I say no more! But the best of it all is that now Monsen is down he’ll drag young Bratsberg after him; and the son will bring the father down——

But of course there’s method even in bankruptcy. You’ll see; I am an old hand at prophecy.prophecy. Monsen will go to prison; young Bratsberg will compound with his creditors; and the Chamberlain will be placed under trustees; that’s to say, his creditors will present him with an annuity of a couple of thousand dollars. That’s how things go, Mr. Stensgård; I know it, I know it! What says the classic? Fiat justitia, pereat mundus; which means: Fie on what’s called justice in this wicked world, sir!
[Pacing the room.] One after the other! Both ways barred!
And now too! Just at this moment!
[Enters from the right.] I congratulate you, chosen of the people!
Elected by 117 votes, and Lundestad by 53. The rest all nowhere.
Your first step on the path of glory, Mr. Stensgård.
And it shall cost you a bowl of punch——
Well, it’s the first step that costs, they say.
[Goes off to the left, shouting.] Punch, Madam Rundholmen! A bowl of punch! The chosen of the people stands treat!
Lundestad, and after him several Electors, enter from the right.
[In a tone of condolence to Lundestad.] Fifty-three! That’s the grey-haired patriot’s reward!
[Whispers to Stensgård.] Are you firm in your resolve?
What’s the use of being firm when everything is tumbling about your ears?
Do you think the game is lost?
[Returning by the left.] Madam Rundholmen stands treat herself. She says she has the best right to.
[Struck by an idea.] Madam Rundholmen—has the best right to——!
The game is not lost, Mr. Lundestad!
[Sits at the right-hand table and writes.
[In a low voice.] Oh, Aslaksen—can you get something into your next paper for me?
Of course I can. Is it libellous?
Well, never mind; I’ll take it all the same.
It is my political last will and testament; I shall write it to-night.
[Enters from the left.] The punch, with Madam Rundholmen’s compliments.
Hurrah! Now there’s some life in the local situation.
[He places the punch-bowl on the middle table, serves the others, and drinks freely himself during the following scene. Bastian Monsen has meanwhile entered from the right.
Don’t be afraid. [Taps his breast pocket.] I have it here.
You’ll deliver it as soon as you can—when you see she’s disengaged, you understand.
I understand. [Calls.] Come, now, the glasses are filled.
You shan’t do it for nothing, I promise you.
All right, all right. [To the servant.] A lemon, Karen—quick as the wind!
A word, Aslaksen; shall you be passing here to-morrow evening?
To-morrow evening? I can, if you like.
Then you might look in and give Madam Rundholmen this letter.
Yes. Put it in your pocket. There now. To-morrow evening, then?
[The servant brings the lemon; Stensgård goes towards the window.
Well—have you spoken to Madam Rundholmen?
Spoken? Oh yes, I said a word or two——
Oh—well—we were interrupted. I can’t say anything definite.
I’ll take my chance all the same; she’s always complaining of her loneliness. My fate shall be sealed within an hour.
[Sees Madam Rundholmen, who enters from the left.] Sh! Not a word to any one!
[Whispers to Aslaksen.] Give me back the letter.
Yes, at once; I shall deliver it myself.
[Stensgård thrusts the letter into his pocket, and mixes with the rest.
[To Bastian.] What do you say to the election, Mr. Bastian?
I’m delighted. Stensgård and I are bosom friends, you know. I shouldn’t be surprised if he got into Parliament.
But your father wouldn’t much like that.
Oh, father has so many irons in the fire. Besides, if Stensgård’s elected, it will still be all in the family, I daresay.
Yes; and I’ve promised to put in a word for him. It’ll be all right. I’m sure Ragna likes him.
[Approaching.] What is interesting you so deeply, Madam Rundholmen?
What do you think he says? Why, that Mr. Stensgård’s making up to——
Yes, but he won’t find the Chamberlain so easy to deal with.
He probably thinks her too good a match for a mere lawyer——
Why, his daughter, Miss Bratsberg, of course.
He’s surely not making love to Miss Bratsberg?
You are quite sure of that?
And he told me——! Oh, I want to say a word to you!
[Lundestad and Bastian go towards the back.
[Approaching Stensgård.] You must be on your guard, Mr. Stensgård.
Against malicious people who are slandering you.
Why, let them—so long as one person doesn’t believe their slanders.
And who may that one person be?
[Slips the letter into her hand.] Take this; read it when you are alone.
[Enters from the right.] Well, I hear you have won a brilliant victory, Mr. Stensgård.
Yes, I have, Mr. Ringdal, in spite of your noble chief’s endeavours.
Like other people, he has a right to vote as he pleases.
It’s a pity he is not likely to retain that right for long.
I mean, since his affairs are not so straight as they might be——
His affairs! What affairs? What have you got into your head?
Oh, you needn’t pretend ignorance. Isn’t there a storm brewing?—a great crash impending?
Yes, so I hear on all sides.
And aren’t both the Bratsbergs involved in it?
My dear sir, are you crazy?
Oh, you naturally want to keep it dark.
What good would that be? That sort of thing can’t be kept dark.
Not a word of it, so far as the Chamberlain is concerned. How could you believe such nonsense? Who has been humbugging you?
I won’t tell you just yet.
Well, you needn’t; but whoever it was must have had a motive.
Yes, just think: is there no one who has an interest in keeping you and the Chamberlain apart?
Yes, on my soul, but there is though!
The Chamberlain in reality thinks very highly of you——
Yes, and that’s why people want to make mischief between you. They reckon on your ignorance of the situation, on your impulsiveness and your confiding disposition——
Oh, the vipers! And Madam Rundholmen has my letter!
Oh, nothing. But it’s not too late! My dear Mr. Ringdal, shall you see the Chamberlain this evening?
Then tell him to think no more of those threats—he will understand; tell him I shall call to-morrow and explain everything.
Yes, to prove to him——Ah! a proof! Look here, Mr. Ringdal; will you give the Chamberlain this bill from me?

lg.l: Yes; it’s a matter I can’t explain to you; but just you give it to him——

div.p: And just add these words from me: This is how I treat those who vote against me!
I say, Mr. Heire—how could you go and palm off that story about the Chamberlain upon me?
How could I palm it off on you——?
Yes—it’s a lie from beginning to end.
No! Is it indeed? I’m delighted to hear it. Do you hear, Mr. Lundestad? It’s all a lie about the Chamberlain.Chamberlain.
Sh! We were on a false scent; it’s nearer at hand.
I know nothing for certain; but they talk of Madam Rundholmen——
Haven’t I prophesied it! She has been too much mixed up with our friend at Stonelee——

lg.l: He drove off this morning before daylight——
And his family is out hunting for him——
And the son has been doing all he knows to get his sister provided for——

div.p: Provided for! “To-morrow” she said; and then her anxiety about her father——!
Hee-hee! You’ll see he’s gone and hanged himself, sir!
Mr. Heire says Monsen of Stonelee——
[Enters from the back.] A dozen of champagne!
Yes, Monsen! Champagne-Monsen! Money-Monsen! Let’s have the wine, confound it all!
Why, where have you dropped from?

I’ve been doing a stroke of business, sir! Cleared a hundred thousand! Hei! To-morrow I’ll give a thundering dinner at Stonelee. I invite you all. Champagne, I say! I congratulate you, Stensgård! I hear you’re elected.
Yes; I must explain to you——
Pooh; what does it matter to me? Wine, I say! Where is Madam Rundholmen?
[Makes a motion to go out to the left.
[Who has just entered, intercepts him.] No one can see the mistress just now; she’s got a letter——
Yes; and it seems quite to have upset her.
Good-bye, Mr. Monsen; dinner at Stonelee to-morrow——?
[Whispers.] Mr. Heire, will you do me a service?
Then just run me down a little to Madam Rundholmen; indulge in an innuendo or two at my expense. You are so good at that sort of thing.
What the deuce is the meaning of this?
I have my reasons. It’s a joke, you know—a wager with—with some one you have a grudge against.
Aha, I understand. I say no more!
Don’t go too far, you know. Just place me in a more or less equivocal light—make her a little suspicious of me, for the moment.
Rely upon me; it will be a real pleasure to me.
Thanks, thanks in advance. [Goes towards the table.] Mr. Lundestad, we shall meet to-morrow forenoon at the Chamberlain’s.
You needn’t. Henceforth I will be my own counsellor.
[At the punch-bowl.] Another glass, Aslaksen! Where’s Bastian?
He’s just gone out. But I have a letter to deliver for him.
But not till to-morrow evening, he said; to-morrow evening, neither sooner nor later. Here’s to you!
[To Lundestad.] What the deuce is all this business between Stensgård and Madam Rundholmen?
I suspected as much! But he asked me to run him down a bit—to cast a slur on his character——
I believe he says of you that your word is as good as your bond—and no better.
Hee-hee—the dear fellow! He shall find out his mistake this time.
[With an open letter in her hand, at the door on the left.] Where is Mr. Stensgård?
He kissed your chambermaid and went, Madam Rundholmen!
18. The dollar = four crowns = four-and-sixpence, was the unit of coinage at the time this play was written. It has since been replaced by the crown.
19. “Amtmanden og provsten.” The “Amtmand” is the chief magistrate of an “Amt” or county; the “Provst” is an ecclesiastical functionary, perhaps equivalent to a rural dean.
20. Bastian now says “thou” (du) to Stensgård—il le tutoie.

div.head: ACT FIFTH.
div.p: Large reception-room at the Chamberlain’s. Entrance door at the back. Doors right and left.
Ringdal stands at a table looking through some papers. A knock.
Of course you’ve heard the great news?
Do you mean to say you haven’t heard what has happened at Stonelee?Stonelee?
There were ugly rumours yesterday; but then Monsen turned up again; he managed to throw dust in people’s eyes——
Enormous losses in timber, they say. Several houses in Christiania have stopped payment, and so——
And so he has gone off!
To Sweden, probably. The authorities took possession at Stonelee this morning. Things are being inventoried and sealed up——
The son seems to have kept clear of the business; at least I hear he puts a bold face on it.
The tutor brought her and the two little ones here this morning. Miss Bratsberg is looking after them, quietly you know.
And how does she bear it?
Oh, pretty well, I fancy. You may guess, after the treatment she has met with at home——And, besides, I may tell you she is——Ah, here’s the Chamberlain.
[From the left.] So you are there, my dear Doctor?
Yes, I am pretty early astir. Let me wish you many happy returns of the day, Chamberlain.
Oh, as for happiness——! But thank you, all the same; I know you mean it kindly.
One word: be good enough to drop that title.title.
I am an ironmaster, and nothing more.
Why, what strange notion is this?
I have renounced my post and my title. I am sending in my resignation to-day.
When his Majesty was graciously pleased to assign me a place in his immediate circle, he did so because of the unblemished honour of my family through long generations.
My family is disgraced, just as much as Mr. Monsen’s. Of course you have heard about Monsen?
[To Ringdal.] Any further news about him?
Only that he brings down with him a good many of the younger men.
Your son has sent me his balance-sheet. He will be able to pay in full; but there will be nothing over.
H’m. Then will you get my resignation copied?
[Goes out by the foremost door on the right.
Have you reflected what you are doing? Things can be arranged without any one being a bit the wiser.
Indeed! Can I make myself ignorant of what has happened?

Oh, after all, what has happened? Has not he written to you, acknowledged his fault, and begged for your forgiveness? This is the only time he has done anything of the sort; why not simply blot it out?
Would you do what my son has done?
He won’t repeat it; that is the main point.
How do you know he will not repeat it?
If for no other reason, because of what you yourself told me—the scene with your daughter-in-law. Whatever else comes of it, that will steady him.
[Pacing the room.] My poor Selma! Our peace and happiness gone!

There are higher things than peace and happiness. Your happiness has been an illusion. Yes, I must speak frankly to you: in that, as in many other things, you have built on a hollow foundation. You have been shortsighted and overweening, Chamberlain!
Yes, you! You have plumed yourself on your family honour; but when has that honour been tried? Are you sure it would have stood the test?
You can spare your sermons, Doctor. Do you think I have not learnt a lesson from the events of these days?

I daresay you have; but prove it, by showing greater tolerance and clearer insight. You reproach your son; but what have you done for him? You have taken care to develop his faculties, but not to form his character. You have lectured him on what he owed to the honour of his family; but you have not guided and moulded him so that honour became to him an irresistible instinct.

I not only think, I know it. But that is generally the way here: people are bent on learning, not on living. And you see what comes of it; you see hundreds of men with great gifts, who never seem to be more than half ripe; who are one thing in their ideas and feelings, and something quite different in their habits and acts.
